d.title: Three axes, and what each choice costs
d.caption: Every method here explains **the model**, not the world. If a leaking refund column were in the features, permutation importance would rank it first — correctly, because the model does rely on it, and it is an effect of churn rather than a cause.

d.title: Permutation importance, and the two ways to get it wrong
d.caption: Shuffle one column, re-score, and the drop is that column's importance. Two decisions change the answer completely: measuring on the **training** rows reports how much the model memorised rather than how much it relies on the feature, and with correlated columns the shuffle leaves the information available through the copy — so both copies look unimportant and the credit vanishes.

nodes.label: Shuffle one column
nodes.sub: breaks only its link to y

nodes.label: Re-score; the drop is the importance

d.title: Why PDP lies when features are correlated, and ALE does not
d.caption: A PDP varies one feature across its whole range while holding the others at their observed values — which constructs rows that cannot exist, and asks the model to extrapolate into them. On a correlated pair the PDP slope came out **1.58 against a true 2.0**. ALE averages local differences within a bin instead, so it never leaves the data.
cells: the average hides the spread; ICE shows it

d.title: Shapley values: why there is only one fair answer
d.caption: Four axioms pin the attribution down uniquely — that is the result that makes SHAP more than one method among many. The price is the marginalisation over every subset, which is why TreeSHAP's exact polynomial-time algorithm for trees mattered so much.

items.label: Efficiency
items.desc: the contributions sum to f(x) minus the base value

items.label: Symmetry
items.desc: two features that always act alike get the same value

items.label: Dummy
items.desc: a feature that never changes the output gets zero

items.label: Additivity
items.desc: values add across an ensemble of models

items.label: These four admit exactly one solution
items.desc: the average marginal contribution over all orderings

items.label: Which costs 2^p subsets in general
items.desc: TreeSHAP computes it exactly, in polynomial time, for trees

d.title: One customer's prediction, decomposed exactly
d.caption: Tenure 2 months, fee 7.26, four logins, two tickets. The six contributions **sum to the prediction**: base −1.971 plus Σφ 2.423 gives log-odds 0.452, which is P(churn) = 0.611 — not approximately, exactly, because efficiency is an axiom rather than a hope. Four logins a month is the largest single push toward churn at +1.082, and not being a paid-channel customer is mildly protective at −0.077.

d.title: SHAP and LIME are not two implementations of one idea
d.caption: SHAP has a guarantee that its values sum to the prediction; LIME has local fidelity only, and only as measured. The determinism row is the practical one: LIME's top-three features **changed in two of five seeds** on the same row, so a single LIME explanation shown to a customer is not reproducible.

d.title: Anchors and counterfactuals answer the two questions people actually ask
d.caption: An attribution says which features mattered; it does not say what would have to change. A **counterfactual** answers 'what would make this a different decision' — the nearest point across the boundary — and an **anchor** answers 'when does this decision hold' as a rule with a measured precision. Both are directly actionable in a way a bar chart of φ values is not.

nodes.label: Counterfactual says
nodes.sub: the nearest change that flips it

nodes.label: Anchor says
nodes.sub: a rule that holds with 95% precision

d.title: A gradient is a sensitivity, and sensitivity is not attribution
d.caption: The gradient says how the output would move for an infinitesimal change in a pixel — which is a different question from how much that pixel contributed. Saturation is where the two part company: a feature can be entirely responsible for the prediction and have a gradient of almost zero, because the unit it feeds is already flat. Integrated gradients fixes it by accumulating along a path from a baseline, which is also what buys the completeness guarantee.

nodes.label: Completeness
nodes.sub: the attributions sum to the output gap

nodes.label: The baseline is a choice
nodes.sub: black image, blur, mean: it changes the answer

d.title: Four tests that find a shortcut, and they are the same every time
d.caption: A hospital's pen mark on X-rays from the sicker ward; a watermark on one class of stock image; snow behind the huskies; the acquisition channel encoded in a customer id. The cue differs and the procedure does not — and the last test needs no hypothesis at all.

d.title: Attention is not attribution
d.caption: Attention weights say where a representation was **gathered from**, not what moved the output — and the two can disagree completely: a token receiving 85% of the attention had a *negative* contribution to the prediction. The other methods differ mainly in whether they come with a completeness guarantee.

d.title: Explanations as a service, and the budget that decides the method
d.caption: An explanation shown in a product is a latency and consistency problem, not a research one. TreeSHAP is exact and fast enough to run per request; KernelSHAP needs hundreds of model calls and belongs in a batch job. And whatever is served must be **stable** — the same row explained twice must give the same answer, which rules LIME out of the request path entirely.

nodes.sub: an explanation of the old model is wrong

d.title: Every detector is a density estimate in disguise
d.caption: Choosing a detector is choosing which assumption describes 'normal' for your data, and each one's failure mode is a dataset where its assumption is false. That is the whole lesson: a bimodal column defeats the z-score, a curved manifold defeats Mahalanobis, mixed densities defeat the KNN distance.

cells.text: hard to isolate by random cuts

d.title: Masking: the second outlier hides the first
d.caption: The series 10, 11, 12, 10, 11, 13, 12, 50, 52. Grubbs' test gives the 52 a G of 1.82 against a critical 2.22 — **not flagged**, because the 50 has pushed the standard deviation to 17.5. Remove the 52 by other means and the 50 is flagged immediately. The modified z-score flags both at once, because the median of 12 and the MAD of 1 never moved.

d.title: Four planted rows that are ordinary on every column
d.caption: Two features correlated at 0.85, so the normal rows form a thin ellipse. The point (2.5, −2.5) is 2.5 standard deviations out **on each axis separately** — unremarkable one column at a time — and far outside the ellipse. Mahalanobis ranks the three correlation-breakers 1, 2, 3 of 1,004; plain Euclidean distance ranks them 8, 13 and 30, mixed in with ordinary rows. The threshold needs no tuning: under a Gaussian, d² is χ² with p degrees of freedom, so 7.38 is the 97.5% point for two features.

d.title: From a global density to a local one
d.caption: Each step buys the ability to see an anomaly the previous one cannot. A global Gaussian misses a point sitting between two clusters; a KNN distance misses a sparse cluster's members, calling all of them anomalous; LOF compares each point's density with its **neighbours'** density, which is what finally makes 'anomalous for its neighbourhood' expressible.

nodes.label: Flags a whole sparse cluster
nodes.sub: its members are simply far apart

nodes.label: k of 10-20, max over a range

d.title: Three detectors on the churn customers, and what to do with the result
d.caption: An unsupervised detector returns a **ranking**, not a verdict, and the three disagree about the tail because they assume different things about 'normal'. The useful move is to treat the overlap as a priority queue and the disagreement as information: a row that all three flag is almost certainly odd; one that a single detector flags is a question about that detector's assumption.
cells: a random audit sample gives one

d.title: contamination='auto' is not a sensible default
d.caption: With `contamination='auto'` scikit-learn sets the offset to −0.5, so every row whose path is shorter than a random point's expectation is predicted anomalous — **176 of 1,004 rows, 17.5%, for four planted anomalies**. The score distribution's centre depends on the data's shape and dimension, not on how many anomalies it holds. The ranking is unaffected: Spearman 1.000 between contamination 0.01 and 0.1, because it is the same forest with a different offset.

d.title: One-Class SVM draws a boundary; Isolation Forest counts cuts
d.caption: Two opposite strategies. The SVM learns a **surface** enclosing the normal region, so its answer depends on a kernel width and a ν that bounds the fraction outside — and it degrades badly in high dimension. Isolation Forest never models normality at all: it splits at random and measures how **few cuts** isolate a row, which is cheap, scales linearly and needs no distance metric.

d.title: Reconstruction error: anomalous means 'not expressible'
d.caption: Compress and rebuild; the rows that rebuild badly are the ones the compression had no language for. Three failure modes follow directly from that framing: a network wide enough to learn the identity reconstructs **everything** perfectly, a trivially simple input reconstructs perfectly whether or not it is normal, and anomalies present in the training data get learned and then reconstructed happily.

nodes.label: No real bottleneck
nodes.sub: it learns the identity: all errors ~ 0

d.title: COPOD and ECOD: tail probabilities, and nothing to tune
d.caption: Both estimate each column's empirical distribution and score a row by how far into the **tails** its values sit, combining the per-column tail probabilities. That makes them parameter-free, scale-free and fast — and blind to exactly what Mahalanobis sees, because a row ordinary in every marginal but impossible as a combination has no extreme tail anywhere.

d.title: Setting a threshold when there are no labels
d.caption: Without labels there is no optimum to find, so the threshold must come from somewhere outside the data — and review capacity is the honest answer in almost every production system. The random audit sample is the part that is usually missing: without it the base rate is unknown, and a supervised model trained on the queue learns only the queue's biases.
cells: a rate, if the assumption holds

d.title: Streaming: the reference window is a model that has to be refitted
d.caption: A detector trained once drifts into uselessness, because yesterday's normal becomes today's anomaly and the other way round. The loop below is the production shape — and the dangerous step is the refit: fit the new reference on a window that already contains the attack and the detector learns to accept it, so the window needs the same review as the model.

d.title: A fraud system, end to end, and the two feedback paths
d.caption: The upper path is the queue, and it only ever teaches you **precision** — analysts verdict the rows you chose to show them. The lower path is what makes recall knowable: a random audit sample nobody selected, plus chargebacks that arrive weeks later. Without both, the supervised model trained on this data learns the queue's biases and nothing about the frauds the queue never surfaced.
